Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Trojanized NuGet typosquat 'Newtonsoftt.Json.Net' restored into a .NET build · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Newtonsoftt.Json.Net trojan C2/exfil beacon to 185.126.237.64:5341 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Trojanized NuGet typosquat 'Newtonsoftt.Json.Net' restored into a .NET build AIDelivery High
Hunts for the specific malicious Newtonsoft.Json fork 'Newtonsoftt.Json.Net' (double-t typosquat) being pulled from NuGet and unpacked into a developer or build-server package cache. This is the initial-access foothold for the Digitain FG-Crash game-rigging supply-chain attack; the package name is unique and never appears in a clean environment. Rationale: Uses the exact typosquat package name 'Newtonsoftt.Json.Net' (double-t) called out by JFrog and confirmed by The Hacker News; the name is unique to this campaign so any file-cache write of it is high-fidelity. Corroborated against JFrog's original research. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/trojanized-newtonsoftjson-fork-hides.html • https://jfrog.com/blog/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher intentionally downloading the sample for analysis into a sandbox
  • A threat-intel or SOAR enrichment job caching the .nupkg for detonation
  • A blocklist/allowlist automation writing the package name into a report file (matches on path but not a real install)
  • A developer who deliberately references the package while reproducing the advisory
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe") and FolderPath !has @"\Sandbox\" and FolderPath !has @"\Quarantine\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the write path is a real package cache (~/.nuget/packages, build agent workspace) versus an analyst sandbox; capture the exact version folder (11.0.4–11.0.11) and the initiating process (dotnet.exe/nuget.exe/msbuild.exe). 2) Contain: quarantine the package folder, purge it from the offending cache/feed, and pin Newtonsoft.Json to a known-good version via packages.lock.json; block downstream builds from restoring it. 3) Hunt: on the same host and any build server that consumed this artifact, pivot to UC2 for outbound connections to 185.126.237.64:5341 to confirm whether the payload detonated on a Digitain FG-Crash backend.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "newtonsoftt.json.net" or FileName startswith "newtonsoftt.json.net"
| where FileName endswith ".nupkg" or FileName endswith ".dll" or FolderPath has @"\.nuget\packages\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "newtonsoftt.json.net" or TargetFileName startswith "newtonsoftt.json.net"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*newtonsoftt.json.net*" OR Filesystem.file_name="newtonsoftt.json.net*.nupkg") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Newtonsoftt.Json.Net trojan C2/exfil beacon to 185.126.237.64:5341 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts for outbound connections to the hard-coded exfiltration endpoint 185.126.237.64 on TCP 5341 used by the Newtonsoftt.Json.Net trojan to ship rigged FG-Crash round results disguised as telemetry. This confirms the payload actually detonated (target-specific), not merely that the package was installed. Rationale: Uses the hard-coded C2/exfil IOC 185.126.237.64:5341 stated in the article and confirmed by JFrog; the unusual high port + fixed IP is high-fidelity. The malware also tags traffic with the custom header 'X-Seq-ApiKey: theperfectheist2025' — add that as a proxy/web-gateway enrichment where full HTTP header logging exists. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/trojanized-newtonsoftjson-fork-hides.html • https://jfrog.com/blog/
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel analyst deliberately detonating the sample and beaconing to the sink IP from a sandbox
  • A blue-team purple-team exercise replaying the IOC
  • A honeypot or deception host configured to attract the C2
  • Automated IOC connectivity/health checks that probe known-bad IPs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox" and DeviceName !has "honeypot"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (should be a .NET host process that loaded the trojan JSON assembly) and confirm the host previously restored Newtonsoftt.Json.Net (pivot to UC1); capture destination bytes and periodicity. 2) Contain: block 185.126.237.64:5341 at the perimeter firewall/EDR, isolate the host if it is an FG-Crash/Digitain backend, and snapshot memory before reboot. 3) Hunt: search proxy/web-gateway logs for the custom header 'X-Seq-ApiKey: theperfectheist2025', review FG-Crash round-outcome data for statistical manipulation, and sweep all build servers that consumed the package for the same egress.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "185.126.237.64" and RemotePort == 5341
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "185.126.237.64" and DestinationPort == 5341
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\onenote.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\mspub.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\visio.exe"

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SecurityEvent

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Azure DevOps MCP Flaw Lets Hidden PR Comments Hijack AI Review Agents

The Hacker News
2026-07-22 12 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A single invisible comment in an Azure DevOps pull request can turn a reviewer's own AI coding agent against them, driving it into projects the attacker has no rights to reach and quietly leaking what it finds. The flaw is in Microsoft's official Azure DevOps MCP server, and it works because one of its tools returns pull request descriptions without a prompt-injection guardrail the company had

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190 T1195.002 T1486 T1528 T1555.003 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Azure DevOps MCP server launched without least-privilege domain scope (no -d flag) · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Azure DevOps MCP server loaded with abusable pipelines/wiki/security domains in a review context · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Azure DevOps MCP server launched without least-privilege domain scope (no -d flag) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts developer/CI endpoints running Microsoft's official @azure-devops/mcp server with a broad token and NO -d domain restriction, which is the exact posture Manifold Security says concentrates the confused-deputy risk: a hidden PR-description comment can then drive the reviewer's agent across pipelines, wikis, repos and work items it never needed. Article-specific because it keys on the real package name and the -d least-privilege flag Microsoft documents. Rationale: Keys on the confirmed npm package name @azure-devops/mcp and the -d least-privilege flag from Microsoft's own GETTINGSTARTED docs; a broad token with no -d is the precise risk-concentration posture Manifold and THN describe. Cross-checked microsoft/azure-devops-mcp repo docs and the THN write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-azure-devops-mcp-flaw-lets.html • https://github.com/microsoft/azure-devops-mcp/blob/main/docs/GETTINGSTARTED.md • https://www.npmjs.com/package/@azure-devops/mcp
ATT&CKT1204 T1078
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DevOps engineer intentionally running the full-scope MCP server for general Azure DevOps automation (not code review) where broad tooling is acceptable
  • Self-hosted Azure Pipelines build agent (Agent.Worker.exe/Agent.Listener.exe) launching the server with a service PAT for CI tasks
  • Initial one-time setup/testing of the MCP server before an operator adds -d scoping
  • Solo/hobby repos with no external contributors, where an over-scoped token carries no real confused-deputy exposure
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("agent.worker.exe", "agent.listener.exe")   // exclude self-hosted Azure Pipelines build agents running the server for CI
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the token/PAT scope the server was started with and whether the same host runs a coding agent (Copilot CLI, Claude Code, node) in an auto-approve posture with no per-tool prompts. 2) Contain: re-launch the server with `-d` limited to the domains the task needs (e.g. `-d core repositories work-items`) and drop pipelines/wiki/comment-posting from any code-review tool set; downscope the PAT to the project under review and enable per-tool approval. 3) Hunt: pull Azure DevOps audit logs for cross-project pipeline runs, wiki reads, or PR comments posted by this user during reviews, and scan open PR descriptions for hidden HTML comments (`<!-- ... -->`) that could carry an injection payload.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "@azure-devops/mcp"
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has "-d")   // -d flag = per-domain least-privilege scoping; absence loads ALL domains
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          Agent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          Runtime = FileName,
          ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "@azure-devops/mcp"
| where not(CommandLine has "-d")   // no per-domain restriction = broad token, full tool surface
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Azure DevOps MCP Server Launched Without Least-Privilege Domain Scope
id: 7463d74f-5fd7-4d25-afee-bc9ca57cbd59
status: experimental
description: Detects the official @azure-devops/mcp server started without the -d domain flag, exposing the full pipelines/wiki/repos/work-items tool surface an injected PR comment can abuse.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-azure-devops-mcp-flaw-lets.html
  - https://github.com/microsoft/azure-devops-mcp/blob/main/docs/GETTINGSTARTED.md
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/22
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1204
  - attack.t1078
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    CommandLine|contains: '@azure-devops/mcp'
  filter_scoped:
    CommandLine|contains: ' -d '
  condition: selection and not filter_scoped
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @CommandLine:*azure-devops/mcp* NOT @CommandLine:*\-d\ *
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/@azure-devops\/mcp/i
| NOT CommandLine=/\s-d\s/i
| table([ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine])
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*@azure-devops/mcp*" AND NOT Processes.process="* -d *" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*@azure-devops/mcp*" AND NOT Processes.process="* -d *" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Azure DevOps MCP server loaded with abusable pipelines/wiki/security domains in a review context AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts endpoints where @azure-devops/mcp is explicitly scoped (via -d) to include the pipelines, wiki, or advanced-security domains — the exact tools Manifold's PoC chained (trigger a pipeline in another project, read a confidential wiki, post it back as a PR comment). A code-review tool set has no legitimate need for these, so their presence is the abusable surface. Distinct pivot from UC1: positive match on the loaded-domain tokens rather than absence of -d. Rationale: Positively matches the pipelines/wiki/advanced-security domain tokens that Manifold's PoC chain actually exercised (pipeline trigger -> confidential wiki read -> PR-comment exfil), grounded in the real -d domain names from Microsoft's docs. Cross-checked the microsoft/azure-devops-mcp docs and THN article. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-azure-devops-mcp-flaw-lets.html • https://github.com/microsoft/azure-devops-mcp/blob/main/docs/GETTINGSTARTED.md
ATT&CKT1213 T1204
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate release/pipeline automation where the operator genuinely needs the pipelines domain and there is no untrusted-PR review workflow
  • Documentation or wiki-maintenance agents that intentionally load the wiki domain
  • Security teams using the advanced-security domain for CodeQL/alert triage rather than PR review
  • One-off broad-scope invocation by a DevOps engineer exploring MCP tooling
  • Full-scope launches with no -d at all that also happen to log these domain names via server startup banners (validate the token appears as a CLI arg, not stdout)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("agent.worker.exe", "agent.listener.exe")   // exclude self-hosted Azure Pipelines build agents
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify whether this host runs an interactive code-review agent and whether the loaded pipelines/wiki/advanced-security domains are actually required for that workflow; confirm auto-approve (no per-tool prompt) posture. 2) Contain: re-scope the server to only the domains the task needs and strip pipeline-run, wiki-read, and comment-post tools from the review tool set; require per-tool approval so an odd cross-project pipeline run is caught before it fires. 3) Hunt: in Azure DevOps audit logs, correlate this user/PAT for a pipeline run in one project plus a wiki read plus a PR comment within the same review window (the PoC signature), and grep recent PR descriptions for hidden `<!-- -->` HTML comments.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "@azure-devops/mcp"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pipelines", "wiki", "advanced-security")   // domains abused in Manifold PoC; not needed by a code-review agent
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          Agent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "@azure-devops/mcp"
| where CommandLine has_any ("pipelines", "wiki", "advanced-security")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

SecurityEvent

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'

            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

CloudAppEvents

          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent

AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result

APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Anomalous POST to SharePoint /_trust/default.aspx WS-Federation endpoint (CVE-2026-50522) · [LLM] SharePoint w3wp.exe spawning command shells / LOLBins (deserialization RCE execution) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

Anomalous POST to SharePoint /_trust/default.aspx WS-Federation endpoint (CVE-2026-50522) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-50522 exploitation entrypoint: an HTTP POST to SharePoint's '/_trust/default.aspx' WS-Federation sign-in endpoint carrying an oversized serialized SecurityContextToken cookie. Normal federated sign-in posts are small; the malicious .NET BinaryFormatter payload inflates the request body, so a POST to this exact endpoint with a large request size is a high-fidelity exploit signal. Rationale: Uses the exact endpoint named in the article ('/_trust/default.aspx') plus the WS-Federation POST method; the >8000-byte request-size floor separates the oversized serialized SecurityContextToken payload from routine federated sign-ins. Cross-checked against watchTowr/BleepingComputer and the analogous 2025 ToolShell chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/critical-sharepoint-rce-flaw-exploited-to-steal-machine-keys/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/critical-sharepoint-rce-cve-2026-50522.html • https://securityaffairs.com/195760/security/public-poc-triggers-active-exploitation-of-critical-sharepoint-rce-vulnerability-cve-2026-50522.html
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate ADFS / third-party IdP federated sign-in posting a large SAML/WS-Fed token to the trust endpoint
  • Load-balancer or synthetic-monitoring health checks replaying captured sign-in requests
  • Large but benign SecurityContextToken from a heavily group-membership-loaded user
  • Security scanners / vuln assessment tools (Nessus, Qualys) probing the endpoint post-disclosure
Suppression filter
| where cIP !startswith "10." and cIP !startswith "192.168." and cIP !startswith "172.16."
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full W3CIISLog rows for the source IP — confirm it is external/untrusted and not your ADFS proxy, and inspect scStatus (200/500 = payload processed/errored). 2) Contain: if the source is not a known IdP, block the IP at the WAF/edge and confirm the July SharePoint updates are installed; isolate the SharePoint server if a shell spawn (UC2) correlates. 3) Hunt: pivot to DeviceProcessEvents for w3wp.exe child processes and to machine-key/web.config access (UC2, UC3) on the same host within minutes of the POST, and rotate SharePoint machine keys per watchTowr guidance.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where csUriStem =~ "/_trust/default.aspx"
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csBytes > 8000   // serialized BinaryFormatter SecurityContextToken cookies are large; genuine WS-Fed posts are typically < 4KB
| summarize Requests=count(), Statuses=make_set(scStatus), UserAgents=make_set(csUserAgent), MaxReqBytes=max(csBytes), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by cIP, Computer, sSiteName
| order by MaxReqBytes desc

SharePoint w3wp.exe spawning command shells / LOLBins (deserialization RCE execution) AIExploitation High
Detects the post-exploitation execution stage of CVE-2026-50522: the SharePoint IIS worker process w3wp.exe spawning cmd.exe, PowerShell, or download LOLBins. A vulnerable BinaryFormatter deserialization path yields arbitrary code under w3wp.exe, and w3wp spawning an interactive shell is abnormal in legitimate SharePoint operation. Rationale: w3wp.exe (the SharePoint/IIS worker) spawning cmd/PowerShell/LOLBins is the direct on-host manifestation of the article's 'arbitrary code execution on the SharePoint server' and matches the confirmed 2025 ToolShell behaviour; parent-child pinning keeps FPs near zero. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/critical-sharepoint-rce-flaw-exploited-to-steal-machine-keys/ • https://ctid.mitre.org/blog/2025/08/04/lessons-from-sharepoint-vulnerability-cve-2025-53770/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/07/22/disrupting-active-exploitation-of-on-premises-sharepoint-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint timer/PSConfig maintenance or patch scripts legitimately invoking PowerShell under the app-pool identity during an upgrade window
  • Administrator running Get-SPProduct / STSADM diagnostics inside an IIS-hosted admin page
  • Third-party SharePoint add-in or monitoring agent that shells out from w3wp
  • SCOM/backup agents launching cmd.exe under the worker process
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Microsoft.SharePoint.Administration","PSConfig","stsadm","Get-SPProduct") and AccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child ProcessCommandLine and grandparent chain — decode any base64/-EncodedCommand and check whether it references machine keys, web.config, or outbound URLs. 2) Contain: kill the process tree, isolate the SharePoint host from the network, and preserve w3wp memory; disable the affected web app pool if active exploitation is confirmed. 3) Hunt: correlate backward to a UC1 POST on /_trust/default.aspx and forward to machine-key/web.config access (UC3) and any new .aspx files or IIS module drops; rotate SharePoint machine keys and forced-re-auth all users.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","regsvr32.exe","rundll32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharePoint machine-key / web.config theft via w3wp-spawned process (CVE-2026-50522 persistence) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the credential-access stage of CVE-2026-50522: a process spawned by w3wp.exe reading or referencing SharePoint machine keys (ValidationKey/DecryptionKey in web.config / machine.config). Stealing these keys lets the attacker forge valid authentication tokens and retain access after patching, so machine-key access from the IIS worker context is the persistence pivot. Rationale: Directly targets the article's core impact — 'stealing machine keys' to forge auth tokens and survive patching — by flagging w3wp-child processes touching ValidationKey/DecryptionKey/web.config; these config strings under the IIS worker context are rarely benign and match confirmed ToolShell machine-key extraction. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/critical-sharepoint-rce-flaw-exploited-to-steal-machine-keys/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/07/22/disrupting-active-exploitation-of-on-premises-sharepoint-vulnerabilities/ • https://ctid.mitre.org/blog/2025/08/04/lessons-from-sharepoint-vulnerability-cve-2025-53770/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1606.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint farm configuration or PSConfig upgrade legitimately reading/writing web.config under the app-pool identity
  • Administrator running Set-SPMachineKey / key-rotation scripts during remediation
  • Backup or DR tooling copying web.config as part of a farm export
  • Config-management agent (DSC/Ansible) templating machine.config on the server
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("PSConfig","Update-SPMachineKey","Set-SPMachineKey") and AccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the exact ProcessCommandLine — determine whether it reads (theft) or writes (attacker-set key) and whether the parent w3wp child chain traces to a UC2 shell spawn. 2) Contain: isolate the host, and IMMEDIATELY rotate SharePoint machine keys (Update-SPMachineKey + IISReset across the farm) since stolen keys survive patching; invalidate existing sessions. 3) Hunt: search Entra/ADFS and SharePoint sign-ins for forged-token reuse (unusual token issuance, impossible travel, service-account access anomalies) after the exploitation window, and audit for new .aspx web shells and IIS modules.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("machineKey","ValidationKey","DecryptionKey","web.config","machine.config","Get-SPMachineKey")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessId, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("machineKey","ValidationKey","DecryptionKey","web.config","machine.config","Get-SPMachineKey")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Kratos PhaaS network/DNS egress to phishing domains and operator IP 41.128.0.142 AIDelivery Medium
Hunts endpoint or perimeter contact with the seized Kratos phishing-as-a-service domains and the Egyptian operator IP 41.128.0.142. Article-specific because it keys on the exact domain set and shared operator IP tied to the fake Microsoft 365 login infrastructure. Rationale: Uses the article's exact seized Kratos domain set plus operator IP 41.128.0.142, both confirmed by ANY.RUN's Kratos write-up which maps them to the fake M365 login infrastructure. IOC-anchored, so FP is essentially limited to sinkhole/researcher traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/kratos-phaas-account-takeover/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/german-authorities-dismantle-kratos-phishing-as-a-service-infrastructure • https://www.presseportal.de/blaulicht/pm/7/6318131
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or sandbox detonating the phishing URL from a corporate host
  • Threat-intel/sinkhole crawlers hosted in the environment resolving the domains
  • A .de/.es compromised-but-legitimate WordPress site (e.g. crm-technik.de) being visited for benign reasons after cleanup
  • URL-scanning email gateway or Safe Links backend detonation traffic
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","MpCmdRun.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("safelinks","urldetonation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/host that resolved or connected, pull the InitiatingProcess (expect a browser) and confirm it was a real user session vs. a scanner. 2) Contain: if a real user reached a fake M365 page, force an Entra ID password reset AND revoke all sessions/refresh tokens (password reset alone is insufficient — Kratos steals session cookies), block the domains/IP at proxy and DNS. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same user for anomalous sign-ins, new inbox rules, and OAuth grants; check other hosts for the same domain/IP contact.

Kratos phishing kit web-asset fingerprint (barr.svg + lg.svg / PTT-SOft path) AIExploitation High
Hunts the Kratos kit's static-asset fingerprint: a browser session requesting both /assets/img/barr.svg and /assets/img/lg.svg (or the /PTT/SOft/ path, or dsa.svg+sid.gif), which ANY.RUN reports as ~90% recall with near-zero FPs for the fake Microsoft 365 login page. Article-specific because these asset paths and their content hashes are unique to the Kratos kit. Rationale: Uses ANY.RUN's V1 fingerprint (barr.svg + lg.svg in one session, ~90% recall), V0 (/PTT/SOft/) and V2 (dsa.svg + sid.gif); the assets' content hashes (barr.svg 949895df..., lg.svg cd231b89..., styles.css c447e75f..., ani.gif 9d1a1a5e...) are the article's SHA256 IOCs, confirming the kit. Requiring the asset pair, not a single generic file, keeps FP near zero. Cross-checked against: • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/kratos-phaas-account-takeover/ • https://gbhackers.com/kratos-phaas-targets-microsoft-365/
ATT&CKT1204.001 T1566.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign site coincidentally serving files named lg.svg and barr.svg in the same 5-minute window (rare; the pair is the discriminator)
  • Safe Links / URL-scanner backend detonating the phishing page
  • Analyst re-detonating the URL during triage
  • Web-archive / cache proxy replaying the captured page
Suppression filter
| where Requests > 1
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the requesting host+user actually rendered the page (both assets present) vs. a scanner; capture the parent domain hosting the assets. 2) Contain: treat as credential theft — force password reset and revoke Entra ID sessions/tokens for the user, block the host domain at proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: search Entra sign-ins for that user from new IPs (especially 41.128.0.142), review new inbox forwarding rules and OAuth consents, and sweep other hosts for the same asset fingerprint.
DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where RemoteUrl has_any ("barr.svg","lg.svg","dsa.svg","sid.gif","imag.jpg","/PTT/SOft/") | extend Asset=case(RemoteUrl has "barr.svg","barr.svg", RemoteUrl has "lg.svg","lg.svg", RemoteUrl has "dsa.svg","dsa.svg", RemoteUrl has "sid.gif","sid.gif", RemoteUrl has "imag.jpg","imag.jpg","ptt") | summarize Assets=make_set(Asset), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl), Requests=count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 5m) | where (set_has_element(Assets,"barr.svg") and set_has_element(Assets,"lg.svg")) or set_has_element(Assets,"ptt") or (set_has_element(Assets,"dsa.svg") and set_has_element(Assets,"sid.gif")) | order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Url has_any ("barr.svg","lg.svg","dsa.svg","sid.gif","imag.jpg","/PTT/SOft/") | extend Asset=case(Url has "barr.svg","barr.svg", Url has "lg.svg","lg.svg", Url has "dsa.svg","dsa.svg", Url has "sid.gif","sid.gif", Url has "imag.jpg","imag.jpg","ptt") | summarize Assets=make_set(Asset), Urls=make_set(Url) by SrcHostname, SrcUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m) | where (set_has_element(Assets,"barr.svg") and set_has_element(Assets,"lg.svg")) or set_has_element(Assets,"ptt") or (set_has_element(Assets,"dsa.svg") and set_has_element(Assets,"sid.gif")) | order by TimeGenerated desc

Kratos PhaaS credential-exfil POST to next.php / save.php on phishing host AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the credential-harvesting HTTP POST from a victim browser to the Kratos exfil endpoints (/next.php, /nex.php, /n3xt.php, /save.php, /SOft/mini.php) on a known Kratos domain or the operator IP. Article-specific because it pairs the kit's exact exfil filenames with the seized infrastructure, indicating credentials were actually submitted. Rationale: Uses ANY.RUN's documented Kratos exfil endpoints (next.php / nex.php / n3xt.php / save.php / SOft/mini.php with POST params di,pr) anchored to the article's seized domains and operator IP 41.128.0.142, so a match means credentials were actually POSTed — a confirmed-victim signal, not just a page view. Cross-checked against: • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/kratos-phaas-account-takeover/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/kratos-phaas-attacking-microsoft-365-users/
ATT&CKT1056.003 T1539
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate app on a compromised .de/.es host using next.php/save.php naming (mitigated by requiring the Kratos domain/IP)
  • Researcher submitting decoy credentials during triage
  • Automated form-fuzzing / DAST scanner hitting the phishing host
  • Safe Links backend detonation submitting a synthetic credential
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the POST originated from a real user browser session and identify the account; treat any TRUE match as a credential-compromise event. 2) Contain: immediately reset the user's Entra ID password and revoke all sessions and refresh tokens (Kratos steals cookies/tokens — reset alone is insufficient), enforce MFA re-registration. 3) Hunt: review SigninLogs for that account from 41.128.0.142 and other new IPs, check for newly created inbox rules, mail-forwarding, OAuth app consents, and outbound BEC-themed mail to the user's contacts.

Inbound email with URL to Kratos phishing domain clicked via Safe Links AIDelivery High
Correlates delivered inbound email carrying a URL to a Kratos phishing domain with a subsequent Safe Links click by the recipient. Article-specific because it filters on the exact seized Kratos domain set rather than generic phishing heuristics, and flags the click-through that turns delivery into likely compromise. Rationale: Keys on the article's exact seized Kratos domains in delivered inbound email URLs, then joins Safe Links click telemetry to prioritise recipients who actually clicked — high fidelity because the domain set is the IOC and the click makes credential submission likely. Cross-checked against: • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/kratos-phaas-account-takeover/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/german-authorities-dismantle-kratos-phishing-as-a-service-infrastructure
ATT&CKT1566.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Kratos domain that was a compromised-but-legitimate site (e.g. crm-technik.de) also sending benign mail before compromise
  • Internal phishing-simulation campaign reusing a since-seized domain
  • Threat-intel newsletter or IR report email quoting the domain as text (URL present but benign context)
  • Analyst forwarding the phishing sample internally for review
Suppression filter
| where DeliveryAction == "Delivered" and DeliveryLocation in ("Inbox","External")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the message was Delivered (not Blocked/Junked) and whether UrlClickEvents shows a click; prioritise ClickedThrough recipients. 2) Contain: soft-delete/purge the message tenant-wide (ZAP), reset password + revoke sessions/tokens for any recipient who clicked, and block the sender + domains. 3) Hunt: enumerate all recipients of the same NetworkMessageId/cluster, check clicked users' sign-ins from 41.128.0.142, and review for new inbox rules or OAuth grants.
