Microsoft 365 successful sign-in sourced from Kratos operator IP 41.128.0.142 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Alerts on any successful Entra ID / M365 sign-in whose source IP is the Kratos operator IP 41.128.0.142, indicating an operator replaying stolen credentials or session tokens for account takeover. Article-specific because it keys on the single operator IP tied to the seized Kratos backend. Rationale: 41.128.0.142 is the Kratos operator IP (Egypt) confirmed by ANY.RUN; any successful M365 sign-in from it is near-certain account takeover, so it is a clean single-IOC alerting rule with essentially zero legitimate FP. Cross-checked against: • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/kratos-phaas-account-takeover/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/kratos-phaas-attacking-microsoft-365-users/
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1539
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A traveler or VPN egress genuinely using 41.128.0.142 (unlikely — it is dedicated operator infrastructure)
  • Threat-intel enrichment or a red-team exercise deliberately authenticating from that IP
  • Shared NAT if the operator IP were ever reassigned by the hosting provider after seizure
  • Security tooling health-check logins pinned to that address (rare)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the sign-in succeeded (ErrorCode/ResultType 0) and capture the account, app, and conditional-access outcome. 2) Contain: disable the account or force sign-out, reset password AND revoke all refresh/session tokens, require MFA re-registration; block 41.128.0.142 in Conditional Access. 3) Hunt: enumerate all accounts that authenticated from this IP, review each for new inbox rules, mail forwarding, OAuth consents, mass mailbox reads, and outbound BEC mail to contacts.

SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where IPAddress == "41.128.0.142" | where ResultType == 0 | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, ClientAppUsed, ConditionalAccessStatus, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, RiskState | order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c") or SHA1 in~ ("cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c") or MD5 in~ ("cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c") or SHA1 in~ ("cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c") or MD5 in~ ("cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SmartLoader: renamed LuaJIT interpreter launched with .txt/.log data-file stage AIInstallation High
Hunts the SmartLoader execution signature where a batch launcher runs a LuaJIT interpreter (often renamed) passing an obfuscated Lua payload disguised as a text/log/json file (e.g. `start luajit.exe tcp.log`, `vm_s390x.exe lib_bit.txt`). This is the core FakeGit loader trigger and is highly specific to the observed binary+argument pairs. Rationale: Anchored on the exact interpreter+argument pairs published by derp.ca (luajit.exe/vm_s390x.exe/init.exe + tcp.log/lib_bit.txt/icon.txt) — the combination of a Lua runtime executing a text-extension file is not seen in benign software. Cross-checked against: • https://www.derp.ca/research/fakegit-luajit-github-campaign/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/fakegit-campaign-uses-7600-github.html • https://hexastrike.com/resources/blog/threat-intelligence/cloned-loaded-and-stolen-how-109-fake-github-repositories-delivered-smartloader-and-stealc/
ATT&CKT1059 T1036.005 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate game mods or apps that ship an embedded luajit.exe reading a real .log config
  • Developers running Lua/LuaJIT interactively against a local tcp.log test fixture
  • Security tooling that bundles gcc.exe/init.exe for build tasks referencing .txt inputs
  • Renamed portable Lua distributions used in QA automation
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("cmd.exe","explorer.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent chain — confirm the launcher is a Launch*.bat/.cmd and the interpreter sits in a user-writable dir (Downloads/Temp/extracted ZIP), not Program Files; hash the .txt payload. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the LuaJIT process tree, and rotate all credentials/tokens accessible from that user (StealC is the endgame). 3) Hunt: search the same host for the two persistence scheduled tasks and any outbound to polygon.drpc.org or the C2 IPs; sweep the org for the same interpreter+data-file pattern.

   or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "cmd.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("LaunchTool.cmd","LaunchApp.bat","Launch.bat","Launcher.cmd"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("tcp.log","uix.txt","lib_bit.txt","icon.txt","rsp.json","ptd.txt")
   or (ActingProcessName has "cmd.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("LaunchTool.cmd","LaunchApp.bat","Launch.bat","Launcher.cmd"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SmartLoader persistence: scheduled task running a LuaJIT stage or FakeGit task names AIInstallation High
Detects the two daily scheduled tasks SmartLoader creates (names like AudioManager_ODM3 / OfficeClickToRunTask_7d7757) — one runs a cached Lua stage, the other re-downloads a fresh encrypted stage from GitHub. Keys on schtasks creations whose action references the campaign's interpreters/payload files or the specific task-name tokens. Rationale: The two named tasks (AudioManager_ODM3, OfficeClickToRunTask_7d7757) and a task action invoking the LuaJIT interpreter/payload are documented by derp.ca; requiring the action reference the payload avoids FP on the real OfficeClickToRunTask. Cross-checked against: • https://www.derp.ca/research/fakegit-luajit-github-campaign/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/109-fake-github-repositories-used/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Microsoft OfficeClickToRunTask maintenance (excluded because we require the campaign suffix or a Lua payload in the action)
  • Admins scripting scheduled tasks that legitimately run a bundled lua.exe
  • Software installers creating audio-manager helper tasks with unrelated actions
  • RMM tooling creating daily re-download tasks pointing at internal update servers
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the full task action (/tr) and confirm it launches a LuaJIT interpreter against a .txt/.log stage or re-downloads from GitHub; check task author and creation time. 2) Contain: delete both scheduled tasks (schtasks /delete), isolate host, kill running Lua process, and remove the cached stage files. 3) Hunt: look for the loader execution UC on the same host, outbound to polygon.drpc.org / C2 IPs, and query fleet-wide for either task name to find other victims.

| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("luajit.exe","vm_s390x.exe","init.exe","luad.exe","tcp.log","lib_bit.txt","icon.txt","uix.txt","ptd.txt","rsp.json","AudioManager_ODM3","OfficeClickToRunTask_7d7757")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)

| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("luajit.exe","vm_s390x.exe","init.exe","luad.exe","tcp.log","lib_bit.txt","icon.txt","uix.txt","ptd.txt","rsp.json","AudioManager_ODM3","OfficeClickToRunTask_7d7757")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SmartLoader Polygon smart-contract C2 resolution / hardcoded C2 IP callback AICommand & Control Medium
Detects SmartLoader resolving its live C2 via the Polygon blockchain dead-drop (eth_call to polygon.drpc.org against the campaign contract addresses) or beaconing to the resolved C2 IPs 89.169.12.173 / 89.169.12.241. This blockchain-dead-drop resolver is the campaign's most distinctive C2 tradecraft. Rationale: polygon.drpc.org used as an eth_call dead-drop resolver plus the two resolved C2 IPs (89.169.12.173/.241) are corroborated by derp.ca and PlanetJon; blockchain-RPC egress from an endpoint is inherently rare and high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.derp.ca/research/fakegit-luajit-github-campaign/ • https://www.planetjon.net/news/cybersecurity/smartloader-stealc-campaign-blockchain-c2-and-fraudulent-github-repositories/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate blockchain developers / web3 wallets on dev workstations querying polygon.drpc.org RPC
  • Crypto-trading or DeFi desktop apps that use dRPC endpoints
  • Security researchers detonating the sample in a monitored VM
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively resolving campaign IOCs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — a LuaJIT interpreter or unsigned binary hitting polygon.drpc.org/eth_call is malicious; a browser/wallet is likely benign. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 89.169.12.173/.241 and the resolver at the proxy/firewall, kill the process. 3) Hunt: correlate to the loader-execution and scheduled-task UCs on the host, pull any subsequent StealC exfil connections, and rotate every secret on the machine per Island's guidance.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteIP in ("89.169.12.173","89.169.12.241") or RemoteUrl has "polygon.drpc.org"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImNetworkSession
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
 | where DstIpAddr in ("89.169.12.173","89.169.12.241") or Url has "polygon.drpc.org" or DstHostname has "polygon.drpc.org"
 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, Url),
(ImDnsActivity
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
 | where DnsQuery has "polygon.drpc.org"
 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

StealC exfiltration to hardcoded FakeGit gate IPs / PHP endpoint AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the final-stage StealC infostealer POSTing collected credentials to the campaign's hardcoded gate servers 217.119.129.110 / 213.176.72.200 on the fixed path /3d9c1a1d0dc9436eb7b7.php. Confirms successful compromise and active data theft. Rationale: The gate IPs 217.119.129.110 / 213.176.72.200 and the fixed StealC PHP path /3d9c1a1d0dc9436eb7b7.php are documented IOCs from derp.ca; any host reaching them indicates active credential exfiltration. Cross-checked against: • https://www.derp.ca/research/fakegit-luajit-github-campaign/ • https://hexastrike.com/resources/blog/threat-intelligence/cloned-loaded-and-stolen-how-109-fake-github-repositories-delivered-smartloader-and-stealc/
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1555
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel platforms or sandboxes actively probing the gate IPs for enrichment
  • IR responders replaying the sample in an isolated network
  • Blocklist-validation scanners confirming the endpoints are down
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse if the gate server is later repurposed (low, given fixed PHP path)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process and whether an outbound POST occurred; a hit here is a confirmed StealC infection, not a maybe. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately, block both gate IPs, and treat all credentials/cookies/tokens on that endpoint as compromised — force rotation and revoke active sessions. 3) Hunt: back-trace to the loader and scheduled-task UCs, identify what browsers/apps StealC harvested, and sweep IdP sign-in logs for anomalous use of the stolen sessions.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteIP in ("217.119.129.110","213.176.72.200") or RemoteUrl has "3d9c1a1d0dc9436eb7b7.php"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImWebSession
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
 | where DstIpAddr in ("217.119.129.110","213.176.72.200") or Url has "3d9c1a1d0dc9436eb7b7.php"
 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, Url, HttpRequestMethod=HttpMethod),
(ImNetworkSession
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
 | where DstIpAddr in ("217.119.129.110","213.176.72.200")
 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FakeGit GitHub dead-drop stage download by LuaJIT/LOLBin process AIDelivery Medium
Detects SmartLoader pulling encrypted follow-on stages from the campaign's GitHub dead-drop repositories (rd898/package, Mahmudul-Riad/www) when the requesting process is a LuaJIT interpreter or download LOLBin rather than a browser. Catches the mid-chain staging that survives repo takedowns. Rationale: The dead-drop repo paths (rd898/package json/1.json, Mahmudul-Riad/www index/7.txt) from derp.ca are specific; gating on a Lua interpreter or LOLBin as the requester (not a browser) removes benign GitHub browsing noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.derp.ca/research/fakegit-luajit-github-campaign/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/109-fake-github-repositories-used/
ATT&CKT1105 T1102.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately cloning/curling one of the named GitHub accounts before takedown
  • CI pipelines mirroring GitHub raw content via curl/powershell to unrelated repos of similar name
  • Security researchers downloading the stage files for analysis
  • GitHub raw path collisions if the account names are reused after suspension
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("git.exe","code.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process pulling the stage is a Lua interpreter or scripted LOLBin, and capture the downloaded blob (hex/XOR/base64url/AES-ECB chained). 2) Contain: isolate host, block the GitHub raw paths at the proxy, and kill the loader process tree. 3) Hunt: pivot to the Polygon C2 and StealC exfil UCs on the same host; report the still-live GitHub accounts to GitHub abuse and sweep the org for other hosts touching these repos.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Url has_any ("rd898/package","Mahmudul-Riad/www","/json/1.json","/json/2.json","/index/7.txt","/index/8.txt")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Url, HttpUserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("87de3e5a8ef669589c421220cd392ae8027a8f8d3cd97d35ac339f87dcff12c8") or SHA1 in~ ("87de3e5a8ef669589c421220cd392ae8027a8f8d3cd97d35ac339f87dcff12c8") or MD5 in~ ("87de3e5a8ef669589c421220cd392ae8027a8f8d3cd97d35ac339f87dcff12c8")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("87de3e5a8ef669589c421220cd392ae8027a8f8d3cd97d35ac339f87dcff12c8") or SHA1 in~ ("87de3e5a8ef669589c421220cd392ae8027a8f8d3cd97d35ac339f87dcff12c8") or MD5 in~ ("87de3e5a8ef669589c421220cd392ae8027a8f8d3cd97d35ac339f87dcff12c8")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["87de3e5a8ef669589c421220cd392ae8027a8f8d3cd97d35ac339f87dcff12c8"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Gitea vulnerable PR-update API route access (CVE-2026-58443 public-only token bypass) · [LLM] Vulnerable Gitea instance exposed to CVE-2026-58443 (version <= 1.26.4)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Gitea vulnerable PR-update API route access (CVE-2026-58443 public-only token bypass) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP POST requests to Gitea's pull-request update endpoint POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{index}/update, the exact route CVE-2026-58443 abuses so a public-only,write:repository token pushes public base commits into a PRIVATE head branch. Article-specific because the route path, method, and behaviour are the vulnerability signature; correlate the captured source IP / authenticated principal against token scope in Gitea's own admin/audit view to confirm exploitation. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable route from the advisory (POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{index}/update) plus HTTP method — the concrete CVE-2026-58443 signature. Defender/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty: none of those telemetry sets ship Gitea reverse-proxy request paths+methods; token-scope-vs-target-repo correlation must be finished in Gitea's own audit log. Corroborated fixed version (1.27.0) and route via GitLab advisory and multiple vendor write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xxjv-752h-3vp2 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/code.gitea.io/gitea/CVE-2026-58443/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/gitea-vulnerability/ • https://securityonline.info/gitea-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1190 T1550.001 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate maintainers clicking the Gitea 'Update branch' button (calls the same API route)
  • CI/CD service accounts programmatically syncing PR branches with the base branch
  • Automated merge/rebase bots (e.g. renovate/dependabot-style) that update PRs
  • Repository owners updating their own private-repo PRs via a fully-scoped token
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, pull the source IP and authenticated principal from the Gitea admin panel; in Gitea, check whether the token used carried the public-only scope and whether the PR's HEAD repository is PRIVATE while the base (route) repo is public — that combination is the exploit, a same-owner fully-scoped update is benign. 2) Contain: revoke and rotate the offending token, and upgrade Gitea to 1.27.0 (patch #38406); temporarily restrict PR-update to authenticated maintainers if patching is delayed. 3) Hunt: enumerate Actions workflow runs in the affected private repo around the event time (the malicious push can trigger private CI), review git push events into private head branches attributable to that token, and check for secrets exfil in those workflow logs.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)/api/v1/repos/[^/]+/[^/]+/pulls/[0-9]+/update"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Gitea Actions Artifacts V4 HMAC signature reuse across different taskID/artifactName (CVE-2026-58426) AIExploitation High
Detects the defining artifact of CVE-2026-58426: a single V4 artifact signed-URL HMAC (sig=) replayed against UploadArtifact/DownloadArtifact requests carrying two or more distinct taskID or artifactName values. Because buildSignature concatenates artifactName+taskID+artifactID without delimiters, one valid signature is reusable across forged tuples to cross task/repository boundaries — a legitimate runner only ever presents a given sig with one fixed tuple. Rationale: Anchors on the exact vulnerable primitive named in the advisory: the delimiter-free HMAC (buildSignature) means one sig value is valid for multiple (artifactName,taskID,artifactID) tuples. Counting distinct taskID/artifactName per sig against UploadArtifact/DownloadArtifact directly surfaces the tuple-boundary collision the PoC exploits — a signature legitimately binds to exactly one tuple. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-58426 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/code.gitea.io/gitea/CVE-2026-58426/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A single runner legitimately retrying the same DownloadArtifact URL (identical sig AND identical taskID/artifactName) — excluded because both tuple fields are held constant in the true-positive path
  • Reverse proxy / CDN caching layer replaying the same signed request with an unchanged tuple
  • Log duplication where the proxy and Gitea both emit the same request line for one sig
  • Load-test or CI benchmarking tooling issuing many identical signed requests
  • Client retry storms on flaky networks re-sending the same signed URL
Suppression filter
| where DistinctTasks > 1  // require genuinely different task contexts, not sig retries against one fixed tuple
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull all requests sharing the flagged sig; confirm the taskID/artifactName values genuinely differ (not just retries) and identify which repositories/runs those taskIDs belong to and whether they cross a repo boundary. Step 2 (contain): Upgrade Gitea to 1.26.4 (fix line began at 1.26.2); rotate GetGeneralTokenSigningSecret so all outstanding signed URLs are invalidated; suspend the source runner/PAT that issued the reused signature. Step 3 (hunt): For every taskID touched by the reused sig, enumerate its artifacts for unexpected reads (private-repo disclosure) and appended/oversized staging writes; review FinalizeArtifact events for artifacts whose FileSize grew after the forged upload.

| where DistinctTasks > 1 or DistinctNames > 1
| order by Requests desc

Gitea artifact V4 forged over-long artifactID digit string in signed URL (CVE-2026-58426) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the CVE-2026-58426 forgery mechanic where the attacker inflates the artifactID query parameter with concatenated digits (e.g. taskID+attacker-id like 48<attacker artifact id>) so the ambiguous HMAC input suffix matches while the value still parses as int64. Real Gitea artifact database IDs are small sequential integers; an artifactID of 12+ digits on an UploadArtifact/DownloadArtifact URL is a strong forgery signal. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete forgery detail — the forged artifactID carries 'digits that preserve the original HMAC input' (48<attacker artifact id>), producing a value far longer than the small sequential DB IDs normal signed URLs carry. The 12-digit floor is a conservative anomaly threshold that keeps real IDs out while catching the concatenation. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-58426 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/code.gitea.io/gitea/CVE-2026-58426/
ATT&CKT1548.005 T1027
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Very large, long-lived Gitea instances whose artifact table has legitimately reached 12-digit IDs (rare; verify max(id) in the artifacts table)
  • Migrated instances that seeded artifact IDs at a high offset
  • Load/perf test harnesses injecting synthetic large IDs
  • Proxy that URL-encodes and re-emits the parameter, altering apparent length
  • Third-party artifact tooling that pads numeric IDs
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Compare the flagged artifactID digit-length against the instance's real max artifact ID (SELECT max(id) FROM action_artifact); a value orders of magnitude larger confirms forgery. Note the taskID and whether its run belongs to a repo the source principal should not reach. Step 2 (contain): Upgrade to Gitea 1.26.4 and rotate the general token signing secret to void outstanding signed URLs. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate the same source IP/sig with UC 'HMAC signature reuse' to confirm exploitation, and inspect the target task's artifact staging path for unauthorized appended bytes.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has_any ("UploadArtifact", "DownloadArtifact")
| where RequestURL has "artifactID="
| extend artifactID = extract(@"[?&]artifactID=(\d+)", 1, RequestURL)
| extend taskID = extract(@"[?&]taskID=(\d+)", 1, RequestURL)
| where isnotempty(artifactID) and strlen(artifactID) >= 12   // real Gitea DB artifact IDs are small sequential ints; 12+ digits = concatenated forgery
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, taskID, artifactID, ArtifactIDLen=strlen(artifactID), RequestURL
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gitea artifact V4 cross-task DownloadArtifact read fan-out (CVE-2026-58426 private-repo disclosure) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the C:H exploit path of CVE-2026-58426: a single source retrieving V4 DownloadArtifact URLs bound to three or more distinct taskID values within a short window. A legitimate Actions runner only downloads artifacts for its own task context, so one client fanning out across many task IDs indicates URL rewriting to read artifacts from other tasks and private repositories. Rationale: Targets the advisory's independently-scored C:H path ('cross-repository private artifact disclosure'). The pivot is behavioural: DownloadArtifact bound to many distinct taskID values from one source in a minute, which no single legitimate task runner produces, using the literal endpoint and taskID parameter from the vulnerable code. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-58426 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/code.gitea.io/gitea/CVE-2026-58426/
ATT&CKT1213 T1537
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A CI orchestration job that legitimately aggregates artifacts from several dependent jobs (matrix/fan-in workflows) via its own authorized task context
  • Backup or artifact-archival tooling batch-downloading artifacts across many tasks
  • A shared NAT/egress IP collapsing many independent runners behind one SourceIP
  • Gitea admin manually exporting artifacts for maintenance
  • Migration tooling reading all artifacts during an instance move
Suppression filter
| where NOT (SourceIP in ('10.0.0.0/8'))  // optionally scope out trusted internal aggregation runners once their egress IPs are baselined
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Resolve each downloaded taskID to its run/repository; determine whether they belong to different repositories and whether the source principal/runner has grants to them. Confirm the requests reused a signature (join to the HMAC-reuse UC). Step 2 (contain): Upgrade to Gitea 1.26.4, rotate the token signing secret, and revoke the runner registration/PAT tied to the source. Treat any private-repo artifacts read as potentially disclosed. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate all private repositories whose taskIDs appeared; notify owners; review those artifacts for secrets (tokens, kubeconfigs) that now warrant rotation.

| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "DownloadArtifact"
| where RequestMethod == "GET" and RequestURL has "taskID="
| extend taskID = extract(@"[?&]taskID=(\d+)", 1, RequestURL)
| extend artifactName = extract(@"[?&]artifactName=([^&]+)", 1, RequestURL)

| order by DistinctTasks desc

Gitea artifact V4 cross-task UploadArtifact staging write (CVE-2026-58426 I:H) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the I:H exploit path of CVE-2026-58426: a single source issuing PUT UploadArtifact requests bound to two or more distinct taskID values, indicating attacker-controlled data being appended into other tasks' artifact staging context and mutating target artifact metadata (FileSize/FileCompressedSize). A runner only uploads to its own task, so cross-task upload writes from one client are anomalous. Rationale: Targets the advisory's I:H path: uploadArtifact resolves the target by forged task/run/name and appends attacker bytes then calls UpdateArtifactByID. The behavioural signal — PUT UploadArtifact spanning multiple distinct taskIDs from one source — captures the cross-task staging write using the literal endpoint, method and taskID parameter from the vulnerable code. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-58426 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/code.gitea.io/gitea/CVE-2026-58426/
ATT&CKT1565.002 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A single build job legitimately uploading multiple artifacts under its own one task context (only one taskID — excluded by the 2+ distinct-task requirement)
  • Chunked/multipart uploads for a large artifact re-sending PUTs to the same taskID
  • Shared NAT/egress IP collapsing several runners' uploads behind one SourceIP
  • Artifact re-upload after transient failure to the same task
  • Migration/import tooling seeding artifacts across tasks
Suppression filter
| where DistinctTasks >= 2  // one-task multi-artifact and chunked re-uploads collapse to a single taskID and are excluded
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For each taskID written by the source, confirm the task belongs to a different run/repo than the source's own job and check whether the same request reused a signature. Inspect the target artifacts' FileSize growth and staging path for unexpected appended bytes. Step 2 (contain): Upgrade to Gitea 1.26.4, rotate the token signing secret, and quarantine/re-run any downstream job that consumed a mutated artifact via FinalizeArtifact before the write was caught. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate all target tasks/artifacts that received cross-task writes; treat their finalized outputs as tampered and rebuild from clean source; review those pipelines for supply-chain injection into deploy steps.

| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "UploadArtifact"
| where RequestMethod == "PUT" and RequestURL has "taskID="
| extend taskID = extract(@"[?&]taskID=(\d+)", 1, RequestURL)

Inbound X-WEBAUTH-USER header at edge/WAF from non-loopback source (Gitea CVE-2026-20896) AIExploitation High
Hunts HTTP requests carrying an X-WEBAUTH-USER header that arrive at the reverse proxy / WAF from a source IP outside the trusted-proxy range (anything other than loopback). Because the Gitea Docker image ships REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES = * with ENABLE_REVERSE_PROXY_AUTHENTICATION, any client that can inject this header is authenticated as the named user with no password or cookie. Rationale: Keys on the article's exact attack primitive — the X-WEBAUTH-USER header string arriving from a non-loopback source IP — which is only ever legitimate from the co-located proxy (127.0.0.0/8 / ::1). Any external source IP asserting this header is the CVE-2026-20896 impersonation.
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The authenticating reverse proxy itself is deployed on a separate host with a routable IP (not loopback) and legitimately injects the header — tune SourceIP to that proxy's address
  • Security scanners / DAST tools replaying headers during authorized testing
  • A load balancer / service mesh sidecar in the request path that forwards the header on behalf of the proxy
  • Internal health-check probes that spoof identity headers for monitoring
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP != "<your-reverse-proxy-ip>"  // remove this line and instead allowlist the real proxy address if it is non-loopback
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SourceIP is NOT the configured reverse proxy — check the offending request's asserted username (extract from Message) and whether it targets admin/gitea_admin. 2) Contain: set REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES to the proxy's real IP (or 127.0.0.0/8,::1/128) and upgrade gitea to >=1.26.3; block direct network access to the Gitea container port so only the proxy can reach it. 3) Hunt: pivot on that SourceIP and asserted username across Gitea audit logs for repo clones, token/SSH key creation, and admin actions performed while impersonated.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Message has "X-WEBAUTH-USER" or RequestContext has "X-WEBAUTH-USER"
| where isnotempty(SourceIP)
| where not(ipv4_is_in_range(SourceIP, "127.0.0.0/8")) and SourceIP != "::1"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestMethod, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, Message, RequestContext
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Inbound X-WEBAUTH-USER header from non-loopback source (Gitea CVE-2026-20896)
id: 9f2c1a44-7e6b-4d21-b0f2-1c8a4e2b91aa
description: Detects HTTP requests bearing an X-WEBAUTH-USER header from a source IP that is not the trusted loopback proxy, indicating direct identity injection against a Gitea instance with REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES = *.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f75j-4cw6-rmx4
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/22
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1078.001
  - attack.t1071.001
logsource:
  category: proxy
detection:
  selection:
    cs-headers|contains: 'X-WEBAUTH-USER'
  filter_loopback:
    src_ip:
      - '127.0.0.1'
      - '::1'
  condition: selection and not filter_loopback
level: high
APPLICATION
search index=proxy OR index=web ("X-WEBAUTH-USER") NOT (src="127.0.0.1" OR src="::1") | rex field=_raw "(?i)X-WEBAUTH-USER:\s*(?<webauth_user>[^\s,;]+)" | where isnotnull(webauth_user) | stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(webauth_user) as asserted_users by src dest | sort - count
Same Gitea X-WEBAUTH-USER identity asserted from multiple distinct source IPs AIExploitation Medium
Correlation hunt: a single X-WEBAUTH-USER identity value asserted from two or more distinct source IPs within a short window. Under normal reverse-proxy auth a given user's identity is only ever injected by the one trusted proxy; multiple source IPs for the same asserted user indicates direct header spoofing exploiting CVE-2026-20896. Rationale: Legitimate reverse-proxy auth injects each user's identity from exactly one proxy IP; the fan-out of a single asserted username across multiple source IPs is a high-fidelity signal of the header-injection impersonation described in the advisory, and needs no known bad IP to fire.
ATT&CKT1078.001 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A highly-available proxy tier (multiple proxy nodes) all legitimately inject the header from their own IPs — allowlist the proxy pool
  • NAT / egress IP rotation in front of a single genuine proxy
  • Blue-team validation replaying the PoC from several test hosts
  • CDN edge nodes forwarding the header from multiple PoPs
Suppression filter
| where DistinctSourceIPs >= 2 and not (SourceIPs has_any ("<proxy-node-1-ip>", "<proxy-node-2-ip>"))  // keep the >=2 logic but drop legit multi-node proxy pools by allowlisting their IPs
Response runbook
1) Triage: review SourceIPs set for the flagged WebAuthUser — legitimate output is a single proxy IP; multiple public IPs asserting 'admin' or 'gitea_admin' is critical. 2) Contain: restrict REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES to the proxy IP(s), patch to gitea >=1.26.3, and firewall the container port to the proxy only. 3) Hunt: for each spoofed identity, review Gitea actions (new access tokens, deploy keys, webhook creation, repo mirroring) taken from the untrusted source IPs and rotate any credentials that account could reach.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Message has "X-WEBAUTH-USER"
| extend WebAuthUser = extract(@"(?i)X-WEBAUTH-USER:\s*([^\s,;]+)", 1, Message)
| where isnotempty(WebAuthUser)
| where not(ipv4_is_in_range(SourceIP, "127.0.0.0/8")) and SourceIP != "::1"
| summarize DistinctSourceIPs = dcount(SourceIP), SourceIPs = make_set(SourceIP, 20), Requests = count() by WebAuthUser, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctSourceIPs >= 2   // one identity asserted from >=2 IPs in an hour = spoofing, not a single proxy
| order by DistinctSourceIPs desc
APPLICATION
search index=proxy OR index=web ("X-WEBAUTH-USER") | rex field=_raw "(?i)X-WEBAUTH-USER:\s*(?<webauth_user>[^\s,;]+)" | where isnotnull(webauth_user) AND NOT (src="127.0.0.1" OR src="::1") | stats dc(src) as distinct_src values(src) as src_ips count as requests by webauth_user | where distinct_src>=2 | sort - distinct_src
Enumeration of Gitea app.ini config exposing REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects HTTP requests that attempt to read or enumerate the Gitea configuration file (app.ini / custom/conf/app.ini) returning a successful response. Attackers probe for the file to confirm the vulnerable REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES = * default before exploiting CVE-2026-20896. Rationale: Uses the article's named configuration paths (custom/conf/app.ini) and the REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES setting they contain; a 200 on these paths is a strong pre-exploitation recon indicator specific to this Gitea misconfiguration.
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin fetching app.ini through an authenticated admin panel
  • Config-management / backup tooling pulling the file over HTTP
  • Vulnerability scanners in an authorized assessment window
  • A repository literally named or containing a file called app.ini being browsed via the Gitea UI
Suppression filter
| where RequestURL has "app.ini" and RequestMethod == "GET" and SourceIP != "<admin-jumpbox-ip>"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the request path resolved to the real Gitea config (200 with config content) and identify the SourceIP; check whether the same IP subsequently sent X-WEBAUTH-USER headers. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the WAF, ensure the config file is not web-servable, and patch/reconfigure trusted proxies. 3) Hunt: search for follow-on X-WEBAUTH-USER injection (UC1/UC2) from the same source and review any repo access that followed.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where RequestURL has "app.ini"
| where isempty(DeviceAction) or DeviceAction !in~ ("blocked", "denied", "deny")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestURL, RequestMethod, DeviceAction, EventOutcome, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gitea app.ini modified enabling reverse-proxy auth / trusted-proxies wildcard AIInstallation Low
Hunts file writes/modifications to Gitea's app.ini (including the Docker templates at etc/templates/app.ini) on hosts running Gitea. The change that opens CVE-2026-20896 is ENABLE_REVERSE_PROXY_AUTHENTICATION = true combined with REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES = *, so config-file mutation is the persistence/enabling event to audit. Rationale: Grounded in the article's named file (docker/root/etc/templates/app.ini, custom/conf/app.ini) and the two settings whose combination creates the vuln; auditing writes to app.ini surfaces the moment the vulnerable configuration is (re)applied.
ATT&CKT1556 T1078.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Routine container rebuilds / re-deploys that template out app.ini every start
  • Legitimate admin editing app.ini for unrelated settings
  • Config-management (Ansible/Puppet) pushing app.ini
  • Gitea version upgrade rewriting the config
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dockerd", "containerd", "gitea") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("root", "git")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the modified app.ini and check REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES and ENABLE_REVERSE_PROXY_AUTHENTICATION — the dangerous combination is trusted-proxies=* with reverse-proxy-auth=true. 2) Contain: set trusted proxies to the real proxy IP/loopback, restart Gitea, and verify with a curl X-WEBAUTH-USER test from a non-proxy host. 3) Hunt: correlate the modification timestamp against subsequent X-WEBAUTH-USER injections (UC1/UC2) to determine if the window was exploited before you closed it.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "app.ini"
| where FolderPath has_any ("gitea", "custom/conf", "etc/templates")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "app.ini"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("gitea", "custom/conf", "etc/templates")
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gitea webhook/migration SSRF reaching cloud metadata endpoints (IMDS / Azure WireServer) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the Gitea server process making outbound connections to cloud instance-metadata endpoints (AWS/GCP IMDS 169.254.169.254, Azure WireServer 168.63.129.16, or the NAT64-embedded IMDS 64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe) as a result of the CVE-2026-22874 SSRF allow-list bypass. A Gitea web application never legitimately queries instance metadata, so any such egress from the gitea binary is high-fidelity exploitation of the webhook/migration SSRF. Rationale: Uses the exact bypass IPs the advisory calls out (Azure WireServer 168.63.129.16, IMDS 169.254.169.254, NAT64 64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe) scoped to the gitea process; a source-code host reaching IMDS is unambiguous SSRF exploitation. Cross-checked the go-gitea security advisory and Hive Security / cybersecurity-help write-ups confirming the non-blind SSRF and metadata reachability. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/security/advisories/GHSA-2r5c-gw76-rh3w • https://www.cybersecurity-help.cz/vdb/SB2026062240 • https://blog.gitea.com/release-of-1.26.3-and-1.26.4/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team validating the CVE-2026-22874 fix by intentionally pointing a webhook at 169.254.169.254
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanner running under the gitea service account probing metadata endpoints
  • A cloud-native monitoring/agent binary that happens to contain 'gitea' in its path also querying IMDS on the same host
  • Internal chaos/red-team exercise deliberately exercising the SSRF path
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the Gitea webhook history UI and repo migration logs for the affected instance around the connection time; identify which authenticated user created/edited the webhook or triggered the migration and the target URL. 2) Contain: disable the offending webhook/migration, force-rotate any cloud instance-role credentials or Azure managed-identity tokens the metadata endpoint could have leaked, and confirm Gitea is on 1.26.4+. 3) Hunt: review CloudTrail/Azure sign-in activity for use of the potentially stolen role credentials from unexpected IPs, and search for other Gitea egress to the SSRF bypass ranges (100.64.0.0/10, 172.32.0.0/11).

title: Gitea SSRF Egress to Cloud Metadata Endpoint (CVE-2026-22874)
id: 6b1e9a44-2c7f-4d0e-9a3b-8f21e0c7d5a1
description: Gitea process connecting to instance-metadata / Azure WireServer IPs, indicating exploitation of the incomplete SSRF allow-list in webhook delivery or repository migration.
references:

  - https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/security/advisories/GHSA-2r5c-gw76-rh3w
author: SOC Detection Engineering

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\gitea.exe OR *\gitea OR *\Gitea.exe) (@DestinationIp:169.254.169.254 OR @DestinationIp:168.63.129.16 OR @DestinationIp:64\:ff9b\:\:a9fe\:a9fe)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/gitea/i | (RemoteAddressIP4="169.254.169.254" OR RemoteAddressIP4="168.63.129.16") | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.process=*gitea* AND (All_Traffic.dest_ip="169.254.169.254" OR All_Traffic.dest_ip="168.63.129.16" OR All_Traffic.dest_ip="64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe") by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest_ip, All_Traffic.dest_port, All_Traffic.process | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.process=*gitea* AND (All_Traffic.dest_ip="169.254.169.254" OR All_Traffic.dest_ip="168.63.129.16" OR All_Traffic.dest_ip="64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe") by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest_ip, All_Traffic.dest_port, All_Traffic.process | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Gitea process egress to SSRF allow-list bypass internal ranges (CGNAT / 172.32.0.0/11) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the Gitea server process connecting to internal ranges that Go's net.IP.IsPrivate() fails to block — RFC 6598 CGNAT (100.64.0.0/10) and the non-RFC1918 172.32.0.0/11 block — the ranges CVE-2026-22874 lets an authenticated user reach via webhook or migration. Surfaces internal-service probing/exfiltration that isn't a cloud-metadata hit. Rationale: Targets the exact non-RFC1918 ranges the advisory table lists as unblocked (RFC 6598 CGNAT 100.64.0.0/10 and 172.32.0.0/11) scoped to the gitea process — the internal-probing half of the SSRF that a metadata-IP rule would miss. Medium confidence because these ranges have legitimate uses (e.g. Tailscale/CGNAT overlays). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/security/advisories/GHSA-2r5c-gw76-rh3w • https://www.cybersecurity-help.cz/vdb/SB2026062240
ATT&CKT1046 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Organization runs Tailscale or another overlay that legitimately assigns 100.64.0.0/10 addresses to internal services Gitea reaches
  • Legitimate self-hosted webhook receiver or CI runner living in a 172.32.0.0/11 internal subnet
  • Repository migration from a genuinely internal Git host in these ranges
  • CGNAT-addressed reverse proxy sitting in front of an approved webhook target
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIP startswith "100.100.")  // exclude Tailscale MagicDNS/coordination if in use; tune to your overlay's assigned block
Response runbook
1) Triage: correlate the destination IP with the Gitea webhook config / migration target and identify the authenticated user who set it; confirm whether the destination is a sanctioned internal service. 2) Contain: if unrecognized, disable the webhook/migration, and if the response body in webhook history contains sensitive internal data, treat the accessed service as exposed and rotate any secrets it returned. 3) Hunt: enumerate all webhooks and recent migrations across repos for targets in these ranges, and check whether the same user also hit metadata endpoints (UC1).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "gitea"
| where ipv4_is_in_any_range(RemoteIP, "100.64.0.0/10", "172.32.0.0/11")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Connections=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,20) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP
| order by LastSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ipv4_is_in_any_range(DestinationIP, "100.64.0.0/10", "172.32.0.0/11")
| where ApplicationProtocol has_any ("http","https") or DestinationPort in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Connections=count(), DestPorts=make_set(DestinationPort,20) by SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP
| order by LastSeen desc
title: Gitea SSRF Egress to Non-RFC1918 Internal Ranges (CVE-2026-22874)
id: c2f7d3b1-9e64-4a58-b0d2-7a1c4e6f9b30
description: Gitea process connecting to CGNAT (100.64.0.0/10) or the 172.32.0.0/11 block that the incomplete SSRF allow-list fails to deny, indicating webhook/migration SSRF probing of internal services.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2r5c-gw76-rh3w
author: SOC Detection Engineering

  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\gitea.exe OR *\gitea OR *\Gitea.exe) (CIDR(@DestinationIp, 100.64.0.0/10) OR CIDR(@DestinationIp, 172.32.0.0/11))
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/gitea/i | cidr("100.64.0.0/10", field=RemoteAddressIP4) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.process=*gitea* by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest_ip, All_Traffic.dest_port, All_Traffic.process | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where cidrmatch("100.64.0.0/10", dest_ip) OR cidrmatch("172.32.0.0/11", dest_ip) | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.process=*gitea* by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest_ip, All_Traffic.dest_port, All_Traffic.process | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where cidrmatch("100.64.0.0/10", dest_ip) OR cidrmatch("172.32.0.0/11", dest_ip) | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Vulnerable Gitea version exposed to CVE-2026-22874 SSRF (pre-1.26.4) AIWeaponization Medium
Inventory hunt for Gitea installations older than the patched 1.26.4 release that remain exposed to the incomplete SSRF allow-list in webhook delivery and repository migration. Prioritizes patching of internet-reachable Gitea instances before the bypass ranges can be abused. Rationale: Uses the concrete patched version (1.26.4) confirmed by the Gitea 1.26.3/1.26.4 release blog and the CVE id CVE-2026-22874 so the query flags every unpatched instance without a placeholder. Low FP because it is a deterministic version comparison against software inventory. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.gitea.com/release-of-1.26.3-and-1.26.4/ • https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/security/advisories/GHSA-2r5c-gw76-rh3w
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A non-standard build/version string (e.g. '1.26.4+dev' or a distro backport) that trips the numeric parse but is actually patched
  • Forgejo or another Gitea fork carrying its own versioning that the SoftwareName 'gitea' match catches
  • Air-gapped or non-internet-facing Gitea where the SSRF risk is materially lower
  • Inventory lag showing an old version after an already-completed upgrade
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion against the live instance and whether it is internet-reachable or accepts webhooks/migrations from low-privilege users. 2) Contain: schedule/execute upgrade to Gitea 1.26.4+; as interim mitigation, restrict webhook and migration creation to trusted users and tighten the ALLOWED_HOST_LIST allow-list. 3) Hunt: for any instance found vulnerable, run UC1 and UC2 retroactively over the exposure window to determine whether the SSRF was already exercised against metadata or internal ranges.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has "gitea"
| extend Parts = split(SoftwareVersion, ".")
| extend Major = toint(Parts[0]), Minor = toint(Parts[1]), Patch = toint(Parts[2])
| where Major < 1 or (Major == 1 and Minor < 26) or (Major == 1 and Minor == 26 and Patch < 4)
| project DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, EndOfSupportStatus
| order by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-22874" or (SoftwareName has "gitea" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "1.26.4")
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-22874")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-22874")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-22874")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-22874")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

Gitea CVE-2026-56750: automated POST /user/login probing with gitea_incredible remember-me cookie AIExploitation High
Hunts high-rate POST requests to Gitea's /user/login endpoint carrying the gitea_incredible remember-me cookie from a single source, indicating automated probing/fuzzing of the CVE-2026-56750 token-validation path. Article-specific because it keys on the exact vulnerable endpoint and cookie name rather than generic brute-force. Rationale: Keys on the exact vulnerable endpoint (POST /user/login) and remember-me cookie name (gitea_incredible / COOKIE_REMEMBER_NAME) named in the advisory. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch/Datadog are empty because Gitea HTTP telemetry does not land in those; Splunk Web DM lacks a cookie field so it thresholds on endpoint+rate instead. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/code.gitea.io/gitea/CVE-2026-56750/ • https://blog.gitea.com/release-of-1.27.0/ • https://fossies.org/linux/gitea/services/auth/auth_token.go

  • Vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Nuclei) authorised pentest of the Gitea host
  • Load balancer health-check or synthetic-monitoring probe hitting /user/login
  • Misconfigured mobile/desktop Git client retrying login on expired session

| where not(user_agents like "%GiteaHealthCheck%" or user_agents like "%kube-probe%")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SourceIP's full request sequence to /user/login; check whether the UA is a browser or a scanner/library string and whether any attempt returned a session-establishing 302/200. 2) Contain: if non-corporate/unexpected IP, block at WAF and confirm the Gitea instance is >= 1.27.0; if still <1.27.0 prioritise upgrade. 3) Hunt: for any account whose cookie was probed, review subsequent authenticated activity and correlate with the ErrAuthTokenInvalidHash detections (UC2/UC3).

| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/user/login"
| where RequestCookies has "gitea_incredible"
| summarize Attempts = count(), UserAgents = make_set(RequestClientApplication, 5), Statuses = make_set(EventOutcome, 5), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
